Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
2018 Aerial Bighorn Sheep Survey of Known Winter Ranges  
in Sheep Management Areas (SMA) 3 and 4a of the Bow District   
Southern Saskatchewan Region (WMU’s 404, 406, 408, 410, 412, 414, 648, 734 and 794)

More reports online at: https://www.alberta.ca/aerial-wildlife-survey-reports.aspx                                                                
©2019 Government of Alberta  |  Published: July 2019   
Background 
Aerial bighorn sheep surveys are conducted to determine current population trend estimates and herd composition within known winter ranges. The 
last aerial sheep survey was conducted in February 2014 for portions of SMA 3 and the most recent complete surve y of all of SMA 3 and 4a 
occurred in 2011 (See Figure 1 and Table 1).  
 
Sheep disease monitoring during 2016 to 2018 has not detected any evidence of disease concerns within these ranges, while she ep management 
and licensing have remained relatively consistent since the 2011 survey. 
 
More detailed information about sheep management, harvest, registrations, and licensing can be found on at:  
 
 Alberta.ca - Bighorn sheep management: https://www.alberta.ca/bighorn-sheep-management.aspx 
 My Wild Alberta – Hunting Draws Reports: https://mywildalberta.ca/hunting/hunting-draws/hunting-draws-reports/drawn-applicants.aspx 
 
Survey method 
The goal of the survey was to survey all of the 22 known bighorn sheep winter ranges in Sheep Management Area 3 and 4a to produce a minimum 
total trend count of Bighorn Sheep. Extensive review of historical aerial survey sheep surveys was a component of 2018 survey planning to better 
inform winter range habitat, historical distribution of wintering sheep, and to ensure consistent search effort.  
 
The survey was flown from ranges north to south on January 18, 19, 20, 21, (3.5, 3.0, 6.2, and 1.6 hour s respectively) and February 9 (2.5 hours), 
2018 for a total survey effort of 16.8 hours. On January 17, 2018 a ground survey was also conducted for Highway 1A  winter range. A Bell 206 L3 
Helicopter (Ascent Helicopters Ltd.) with rear bubble windows was used with a 3-person survey crew, (Grant Chapman - Lead, Brett Boukall, Anne 
Loosen, Maria Didkowsky, and Mike Grue, Pilot- Greg Goodison) to survey and classify sheep into age, sex, and horn curl classifications.  
 
Classification was further aided by digital photography of sheep groups enabling post flight classification. For this survey,  sheep > 4/5 curl were 
further classified in two categories, >4/5, and >full curl to provide more detail on horn and age structure. All other big game sightings were 
recorded. 
 
Snow conditions were excellent, with temperatures -5 to-15 degrees Celsius and excellent visibility in the mornings of the first 4 days of the survey, 
however, afternoon wind speeds increased to gusting 30 to 60 kilometres/hour and prevented safe flying on the January 18 to 21 af ternoon flights. 
The survey was completed with 1 additional day of flying on February 9 immediately following a fresh, approximately 40 centimetre snowfall with <-
20 degrees Celsius temperatures, clear skies, and calm winds.

Results 
 
A total of 98 groups of sheep were detected ranging in group size from 1 to 38 sheep (mean 8 sheep per group), with a total of 809 sheep 
observed, for the Survey of SMA 3 and 4a. This estimate includes sheep found outside of the 22 known winter ranges and 81 sheep observed 
during a ground count of the sheep wintering on Highway 1A conducted on January 17, 2 018. Of the 98 groups, 83 groups (774 sheep) were 
photographed with a Nikon D3300 24 megapixel camera equipped with a 70-300mm image stabilized lens adequate to determine horn curl and sex 
classification on all sheep (see cover photo for example). This photography enabled enhanced accuracy and confidence in classification of all 
sheep which were first classified in the helicopter and then reclassified via desktop review of >800 images. The total estima tion also includes sheep 
observed in the Ghost Wilderness Area (GWA) which is not one of the historical winter ranges and hence not included in historical comparisons.  
 
A total of 714 sheep were observed, within the 22 historically surveyed SMA 3 and 4a winter ranges. For trend comparison, the se ranges have 
historically averaged 786 sheep (SD of 150 animals) when complete surveys were flown (6 complete survey years 1973, 1978, 1979, 1983, 2000, 
2011). Of the observation in 2018, there were 607 sheep within SMA 3 and 107 sheep within SMA 4a. This 2018 estimate is  less than the 2011 
survey estimate which observed 1000 sheep within these same winter ranges, but well within the range of results. The 2011 est imate was the 
highest estimate recorded since surveys commenced in 1973. Estimates of sheep on specific winter ranges in 2018 showed higher numbers in 
each of Sheep River Provincial Park, Mount Gibraltar, and Mount Head Winter Ranges, and fewer observations at Orient Point, E van Thomas, 
Plateau Mountain, Mist Mountain, and Mount Burns areas. It is currently unknown  what may have caused the difference in the population 
estimates. 
 
The lamb to ewe ratio observed was 40:100 ewes, which is equivalent to the historical mean (41). The total number of rams per  100 ewes 
observed was 47, which is less than the average of 61. The proportion of rams classified as >4/5 curl was fewer that previous surveys, with only 12 
rams observed comprising 2.0% of SMA 3. Within SMA 4a, 0.0% of sheep were classified as >4/5 and full curl (Table 1). However , within the Ghost 
Wilderness Area 12.5% of the sheep were >4/5 curl or full curl (n=8/69). Of the 20 rams classified as >4/5 curl or full curl sheep within SMA 3  and 
4a, 15 were observed within unhuntable portions of the area resulting in only 5 of these rams (1.1% out of 461 total classifi ed sheep) located in the 
huntable portions of the survey area. The low numbers of rams available in SMA 3 and 4a will be evaluated further. 
 
The current ram sheep regulation in effect enables the harvest of Trophy Sheep in a general season with late season archery hunting opportunities 
available via special license in WMUs 410 and 408. Sightings of elk, mule deer, moose, and mountain goats were opportunistica lly collected while 
flying this survey and are summarized within Table 2. Fewer elk were observed tha n in previous surveys. Managers will utilize this survey 
information to continually inform sheep and other big game species management, sustainable harvest, and licensing.  
Ongoing sheep management activities within SMA 3 and 4a include a mineral lick inven tory, disease monitoring and risk assessment, enhanced 
data collection on ram harvest and annuli growth, winter range habitat mapping, and a range condition assessment of Sheep Riv er Provincial Park. 
Winter range habitat enhancement planning is ongoing with implementation of the Evan Thomas Vegetation Management Strategy 2016 -2026 
underway, which includes several prescribed burns.
